Subject: ACME - Performance SLO/SLA follow-up

Alex - great to meet you this morning. Quick recap from our discovery call and the next steps we discussed focused on performance and SLA language so you can take this back to your architecture and procurement teams.

Key items from the call:
- Latency targets: you indicated a goal of sub-200ms p95 for the API end-to-end for short-form streaming responses, with higher tolerance for longer generation windows.
- Throughput & concurrency: target baseline of 150 QPS with spikes to ~600 QPS during peak batch processing windows; expected sustained concurrency of ~300 concurrent active requests (streaming connections counted).
- Streaming requirements: first-byte latency critical for UX. You want partial tokens to arrive as they're generated (server push), and retries/backpressure behavior for unstable client networks.
- Measurement questions: you asked how Redwood measures latency (server-side ingress -> last token emitted vs client-perceived RTT), and what constitutes an SLA breach vs transient slowness.
- Reporting & remedies: monthly SLA reports and dashboards, with defined remedies (service credits) for qualified breaches.

Action items / next steps we agreed on:
1) I'll send a short draft of the SLA language that defines exact measurement points (first-byte, last-byte, percentile windows) and exclusions. Attached is a working draft we can iterate on.
2) Dev will follow up with specifics on concurrency calculation, recommended dedicated capacity, and any headers/flags you can use to exclude test traffic from SLA accounting.
3) Please confirm whether you want p95 or p99 as the contractual target and whether the SLA should apply to hosted endpoints only or dedicated pools as well.
4) If procurement wants, we can produce a short performance test report using a sample workload - let me know preferred test windows.

I attached a brief CSV with the metrics you provided during the call and an initial SLA draft (redwood_sla_draft_v2.pdf).

Thanks - available this afternoon if you want to run through the draft one more time.

--

Thanks, Marissa - helpful recap. A few quick clarifications from our side: 

- Percentile: procurement prefers p99 for contractual SLAs, but engineering is more comfortable committing to p95 for first-byte in streaming scenarios. Can you outline how both would be measured and the difference in expected credit exposure?
- Bursts: our traffic is spiky due to nightly batch jobs and large import events. If we provision dedicated capacity, can Redwood guarantee burst capacity beyond the committed baseline, or is that handled via throttling?
- How is latency measured exactly? Is it measured from the moment the request hits Redwood's edge (ingress) to the first token, to the last token, or both? For streaming UX we care about first-byte p95 and overall completion time p95.
- Exclusions: we need standard exclusions in the SLA (scheduled maintenance, force majeure), but also explicit language for third-party network outages and our own misconfiguration.

Procurement would like to see your draft SLA and an itemized list of credits by severity/percentile. Also, can you include SOC 2 evidence and an ETA on a signed doc flow?

Happy to hop on a short clarifying call - I'm available 11:30-12:30 PT today.

Subject: Re: ACME - Performance SLO/SLA follow-up

Alex - thanks for the clear questions. Below are clarifications we typically include; I've also attached the draft SLA (redwood_sla_draft_v2.pdf) with exact language you can drop into your procurement review. High level answers first, then specifics.

High level:
- Measurement points: Redwood reports both first-byte latency (time from request ingress to emission of the first token/chunk) and end-to-end completion time (time from ingress to final token emitted). Contractual SLA can specify one or both; common approach for streaming UX is to use first-byte p95 as the primary SLA metric and completion p95 as a secondary metric.
- Percentiles: we can offer either p95 or p99. p99 materially increases the risk profile and associated credit exposure. The draft has both options and an example credit table - tell me which procurement prefers.
- Burst capacity & dedicated: for hosted customers, bursts are subject to available free capacity and may be throttled; dedicated pools (reserved capacity) get guaranteed throughput with autoscale policies and optional burst buffers. We'll include explicit language for guaranteed baseline throughput and documented burst handling for dedicated plans.
- Exclusions: standard exclusions included in the draft: scheduled maintenance (we provide 72-hour notice for anything >15m), force majeure, customer-originated or third-party network failures, misuse or abuse (including denial-of-service), and any requests marked explicitly as test/benchmark traffic (see header approach below).
- Reporting cadence & evidence: monthly SLA reports available in the console + historical API access. SOC 2 summary and audit letter can be appended to the procurement packet; I'll loop our security team if you want the full audit report.
- Remedies: typical remedy is service credits calculated as a percentage of the monthly invoice for the affected service. The draft includes tiers by total monthly minutes of breach for the selected percentile. We can negotiate caps per quarter.

Specifics we included in the draft SLA (highlights):
- Definitions:
  • "Ingress" = moment request is received by Redwood front-end and accepted for processing.
  • "First-byte latency" = time from Ingress to time the first token or chunk is successfully emitted by Redwood to the client connection.
  • "Completion latency" = time from Ingress to final token emitted.
  • "Eligible traffic" = production traffic that does not include test/benchmark requests (requests with header X-Redwood-Test: true will be excluded).
- Measurement windows: 30-day rolling window for percentile calculation; percentiles calculated across eligible requests per calendar month for reporting and breach determination.
- Exclusions & maintenance windows: maintenance <=15 minutes is counted; >15 minutes requires 72-hour notice and is excluded from SLA hours.
- Remedies: sample table in draft (example only):
  • p95 breach for >0.5% of eligible requests in a month -> 5% credit of monthly invoice for the service.
  • p99 breach for >0.2% -> 10% credit. Cap: credits limited to 25% of monthly invoice.
- Transparency: monthly report via console + raw metrics export via API (we'll provide a HubSpot link and the raw export for audit).

Next steps I propose:
1) Confirm target percentile (p95 or p99) and whether SLA applies to hosted and dedicated or dedicated only.
2) Dev (cc'd) will reply in this thread with concurrency/throughput guidance and the header to mark test traffic.
3) We'll schedule a 30-min procurement call if needed to walk legal & procurement through the draft.

Available this afternoon for a quick call at 3:00 PM PT or 4:00 PM PT - let me know which works.

Subject: Re: ACME - Performance SLO/SLA follow-up (technical notes)

Alex / team - quick technical notes to clarify how we compute concurrency, throughput and streaming behavior so the SLA language maps to implementation.

1) Concurrency definition:
- For non-streaming requests, concurrency = number of requests actively being processed by our runtime (from ingress to completion).
- For streaming (long-lived connections), concurrency = number of open streams (connections) where we are actively sending chunks. Each stream counts as one concurrent session regardless of tokens emitted.

2) Throughput & tokens:
- Throughput depends on model, context length, and batch efficiency. We size our capacity based on "effective tokens/sec". Example: on a 32k context LLM, one long request can consume equivalent CPU/GPU of many short requests.
- If you're seeing frequent long-context jobs during batch windows, our recommendation is either dedicated pools with higher GPU capacity or splitting large jobs into smaller chunked requests where possible.

3) Burst and autoscaling behavior:
- Dedicated pools: guaranteed baseline throughput (defined in the contract) with configurable autoscale and optional burst buffer. Bursts beyond the buffer will be subject to throttling. We can document a burst SLA for dedicated customers but it increases commitment and pricing.
- Hosted: best-effort burst handling; we provide prioritized routing for customers on higher tiers but no hard guarantees.

4) Excluding test traffic:
- Use header X-Redwood-Test: true to mark flows to be excluded from SLA accounting, or use a tenant-specific test namespace. We'll include this header in the draft and the CSV contains a sample of how we'd filter.

5) Recommended config for your stated load:
- If you expect sustained 150 QPS (short requests) with 600 QPS peaks and ~300 concurrent streams, we recommend a dedicated pool sized for 200 QPS baseline with a 2x burst buffer on demand (or autoscale to peak) - this usually maps to 4x A100 equivalent capacity depending on model. We can provide a cost estimate once we know model choice and average context length.

I've attached acme_requested_metrics.csv (sample metrics you shared) and a short runbook we use for performance tests. Happy to run a short benchmark with your team to validate targets.

--
Dev Patel
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
